 Blyden perfect on Jayhawks’ charmed shooting night
 By Henry Greenstein     Nov 18, 2026
 AP Photo/Abbie Parr 
 Kansas guard Leroy Blyden Jr. (2) celebrates after making a 3-point basket during the first half of an NCAA college basketball game against UNLV in the Players Era tournament, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Las Vegas. 
 LAS VEGAS — Norm Cook knocked down 10 straight shots to open a game against Murray State in December 1973, and Danny Manning matched the feat against Oklahoma State a dozen years later.
 Tarik Black, C.J. Giles, Mark Randall and Lagerald Vick all started 9-for-9 in various games during their own Kansas careers.
 In his fourth official game as a Jayhawk, sophomore guard Leroy Blyden Jr. nearly matched them on Tuesday night against UNLV when he went 8-for-8 overall in a 23-point performance. But he didn’t know about the possibility of chasing the record, of course: “No, I was just playing the right way,” he said postgame.
 During a game in which essentially no one on his team could miss for the first 13 minutes, Blyden was the most efficient of all. Whether he was knocking down three of the Jayhawks’ five 3-pointers on the night or slicing and dicing the Runnin’ Rebels full-court press, he very much looked the part of a high-level scoring point guard.
 He also fed his teammates for six assists and for good measure dished out a metaphorical one or two to Trey Kaufman-Renn and Christian Reeves postgame when asked about his own scoring prowess: “I would just say my teammates just finding me in the right spots … TKR (got) me open, Christian (got) me open, I just knocked down shots.”
 It was clear early on that it could be a good night for the Toledo transfer when he pulled up over UNLV’s Dontrez Williams for a contested midrange jumper — the sort of shot that has been his bread and butter in recent games — that gave KU its first points of the night.
 But he did some of his best work when he operated with pace. He swiped the ball from Williams and got out on the run to set up Tyran Stokes for a transition 3-pointer; soon afterward, Trent Perry gave him the ball on the break in just about the same spot and he knocked one down himself.
 Midway through the first half, he read the eyes of UNLV forward Tyrin Jones like an NFL cornerback and intercepted his pass out of the post, then pulled off a slick move in the lane to score a layup over Cam Miles.
 His game wasn’t all finesse, though. With just under two minutes left in the half, Blyden raced past Issac Williamson after breaking the press and split Jeremy Foumena and Kota Suttle Jr. to score at the rim through a foul by Suttle.
 “They press up a lot on makes and misses, so that’s just leaving transition wide open,” Blyden said. “And you know, every team likes to get wide-open layups, and just layups all game.”
 Then he capped off his 15-point first half with another pull-up jumper on KU’s final offensive possession.
 With the game well out of hand, Blyden made certainly his shot with the highest degree of difficulty in a 72-45 game early in the second half, when Tre White — no stranger to possessing the ball at the end of the shot clock — flipped it over to the young guard instead, and Blyden took a quick dribble to his left before draining an off-balance 3-pointer over Williamson.
 He was simply incapable of missing, in a fashion that created a striking contrast with his 2-for-9 showing against Kentucky in the Champions Classic (even as head coach Bill Self was also pleased with his overall play then).
 “Well, he played great,” Self said on Tuesday, after KU closed out its 102-77 win over UNLV. “You know, he hasn’t shot it well yet. I think against Kentucky he and (Taylen Kinney) were 3 of 18? Is that right? And tonight they’re 12 of 13, or something like that.”
 They were indeed — Kinney went 4-for-5 against the Runnin’ Rebels and scored in double digits for the first time as a collegiate player.
 “So, big difference,” Self said. “But (Blyden’s) a good shooter, he’s a good player, and I thought he shot it great, but more impressively, I thought he played really fast. He looked fast out there to me. And I haven’t seen him look that fast. And maybe it’s because Melvin (Council)’s been out there, but I could get excited about that much speed in the backcourt when we have all our pieces.”
 Indeed, Blyden has taken advantage of his opportunities as a starter while Council, the veteran point guard, has been out with a broken foot. But there’s reason to believe he doesn’t need a starter-level number of minutes to make a difference — after all, his 23 points came in a swift 24 minutes against the Runnin’ Rebels.
 “I thought it was really good,” forward Keanu Dawes said. “That’s actually my roommate on the road, so I was excited to see him do well.”
